planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and direct sow in fall so winter cold and moisture break dormancy naturally; germination follows the next spring as snow recedes.

directions: Broadleaf lupine forms clumps of palmate, wide-leafleted foliage topped by dense spikes of blue-to-purple pea flowers, and it is one of the dominant wildflowers of open Cascades subalpine meadows from Washington south into California. Like most lupines it fixes its own nitrogen and actually performs best in lean, fast-draining soil rather than rich garden beds, so avoid heavy fertilizing. Once established the deep taproot makes it fairly drought-tolerant through the drier part of summer, but plants resent transplanting after the first year, so choose a permanent spot early.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed on the surface in fall and let winter cold-moist conditions trigger spring germination; keep the bed consistently damp since this species naturally grows where snowmelt saturates the soil through early summer.

directions: Sitka valerian carpets moist Cascades subalpine meadows with clusters of small white-to-pale-pink flowers held above deeply lobed leaves, and its musky-sweet scent on warm afternoons is a distinctive feature of high-elevation meadow hikes. The roots and foliage are heavily grazed by bears, marmots, and deer, making it an ecologically important meadow species as well as an attractive garden subject for a cool, consistently moist site. It struggles in hot, dry, or low-elevation gardens and does best where summer soil temperatures stay cool, such as a north-facing slope or a site with late-lingering snow or irrigation.

planting.note: Set out nursery-grown plugs in spring as soon as the ground can be worked, into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil; seed germination is slow and erratic, so starting from divisions or purchased plants is far more reliable.

directions: Western pasqueflower pushes its silky, cream-to-pale-lavender flowers up through retreating snowbanks in Cascades and Olympic subalpine meadows, then produces the shaggy, silvery seed heads that have earned it nicknames like old-man-of-the-mountain. Finely dissected, fern-like foliage and a dense coat of fine hairs on the flower buds help it shed cold and survive brutal late-season frosts right at the snow edge. It is genuinely difficult outside its native cool, high-elevation habitat, needing perpetually moist, sharply drained soil and cool summer nights, so it is best attempted in a mountain rock garden or high-elevation native planting rather than a typical lowland border.

planting.note: Transplant nursery plugs in spring directly alongside an established grass or lupine host, since this species is hemiparasitic and its roots must tap into a neighboring plant to thrive long-term.

directions: Magenta paintbrush brightens Cascades and Olympic subalpine meadows with dense, deep pink-to-magenta bracts atop short, hairy stems, blooming alongside lupines and avalanche lilies as snow recedes. Like other paintbrushes it is hemiparasitic, drawing some water and nutrients through root connections to nearby meadow plants, which makes it notoriously difficult to keep thriving in isolation in a typical garden bed. Gardeners who want to try it should plant young nursery stock next to a compatible native host such as a bunchgrass or lupine and expect a multi-year establishment period even then.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed experiences natural winter chilling before spring germination; plant in a consistently damp spot such as a meadow seep or streamside bed, mimicking the snowmelt-fed ground it grows in naturally.

directions: American bistort (also listed in older references as Polygonum bistortoides) sends up dense, fuzzy, pink-tinged white flower spikes above a basal clump of lance-shaped leaves, forming one of the most recognizable wet-meadow wildflowers of the Cascades high country. Its starchy rhizomes were historically dug and eaten by Indigenous peoples of the region and are still foraged by bears, marmots, and other wildlife in late summer. It will only persist where the soil stays reliably moist through the growing season, so a boggy meadow garden, pond margin, or irrigated bed suits it far better than average garden conditions.

planting.note: Set out small nursery-grown plants in spring into a cool, constantly moist, gritty site; seed needs a long cold-moist stratification and germinates slowly, so starting from plugs or divisions gives far more dependable results.

directions: Subalpine buttercup is among the first flowers to open each year, its glossy yellow blooms appearing on short stems almost at the literal edge of melting snowbanks in Cascades, Olympic, and Rocky Mountain high meadows. The low, compact habit and small, kidney-shaped leaves let it hug the ground and shrug off the cold, wet conditions typical of its brief early-season growing window. In cultivation it demands the same perpetually cool, saturated-but-well-drained root zone found at a retreating snow edge, which makes it a specialist choice for an alpine trough or shaded scree bed with controlled irrigation rather than an ordinary flower bed.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out starts in spring once the ground is workable, in a sunny meadow-style bed with steady moisture; established clumps rebloom reliably through summer with little care.

directions: Subalpine daisy is a mainstay of Cascades and Olympic snowmelt meadows, carrying lavender-to-pink ray flowers with bright yellow centers on wiry stems above tufts of narrow leaves through the short high-country summer. It is far easier in cultivation than many of its subalpine neighbors, germinating readily from seed and tolerating garden conditions well below its native elevation as long as drainage and moisture are reasonably good. Deadheading spent blooms encourages a longer flowering season, and clumps slowly spread by rhizome to form an expanding patch over a few years.
